From Keywords to Entities: The SEO to GEO Shift

For twenty years, we played the keyword game. Find the right terms, optimize the page, build the backlinks, win the ranking. That playbook built careers and companies.

For twenty years, we played the keyword game. Find the right terms, optimize the page, build the backlinks, win the ranking. That playbook built careers and companies.

It's not that SEO is dead. It's that SEO alone is no longer sufficient. A new layer has emerged — and it operates on fundamentally different principles.

Welcome to the entity era.

The Shift in How Discovery Works

Traditional search worked like a librarian: you asked for books about "enterprise data management," and it returned a ranked list of pages containing those words.

AI-powered search works like a consultant: you ask "What should I use for enterprise data management?", and it synthesizes an answer from its understanding of the landscape — companies, products, relationships, reputations.

The difference is profound. Keywords are strings of text. Entities are things the AI knows about.

Keyword Era

  • Pages ranked by relevance to query terms
  • Backlinks as proxy for authority
  • Competition for 10 blue links
  • Success = ranking position
  • Traffic flows to your website

Entity Era

  • Brands recognized as distinct things
  • Knowledge graphs as source of truth
  • Competition for AI mentions
  • Success = citation quality
  • Answers delivered in the AI response

What is an Entity?

Entity Definition

In AI terms, an entity is a distinct, recognizable thing — a company, product, person, concept, or place — that exists in the model's knowledge representation.

Entities have attributes (founding date, headquarters, employee count) and relationships (competitors, partners, customers, categories).

When you're an established entity, AI can reason about you. When you're not, you're just text on a page.

Google's Knowledge Graph, Wikidata, and the training data of large language models all maintain entity databases. If you exist in these systems, AI can:

  • Recognize mentions of your brand even with variations in naming
  • Associate you with your category automatically
  • Connect you to related entities (customers, partners, competitors)
  • Surface you in response to relevant queries

If you don't exist as an entity, you're dependent on keyword matching — and that's increasingly unreliable as queries become conversational.

The Evolution of Search

1998-2010: The Keyword Era

Google dominates with PageRank. SEO = keywords + backlinks. Success measured in SERP position.

2012: Knowledge Graph Launch

Google introduces entity understanding. Search results start showing structured data, not just links.

2019: BERT and Semantic Search

Google understands natural language queries. Long-tail keywords matter less; intent matters more.

2023: ChatGPT and AI Search

Conversational AI becomes mainstream. Users get answers, not links. GEO emerges as a discipline.

2025-2026: AI-First Discovery

AI Overviews, Perplexity, and conversational search become primary research tools. Entity presence is mandatory.

Why Keywords Still Matter (But Differently)

This isn't about abandoning SEO. Keywords still matter for:

  • Traditional search: Google still processes billions of keyword-based queries daily
  • Content discovery: Keywords help AI find and index your content initially
  • Category association: Using consistent category terms helps establish entity relationships

But keywords alone don't create entity recognition. You can rank #1 for "enterprise data management software" and still be invisible in AI responses if you haven't established yourself as a known entity.

"Optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience, and thus still SEO. But the tactics have evolved. Entity clarity, structured data, and authoritative sources now matter more than keyword density." — Google's 2026 GEO Documentation

Building Entity Presence

Becoming a recognized entity requires deliberate effort:

1. Establish Your Entry Points

  • Wikidata: Create entries for your company and products. This feeds Knowledge Graphs.
  • Wikipedia: If you meet notability criteria, a Wikipedia page is the gold standard.
  • Schema markup: Add Organization and Product schemas to tell AI what you are.

2. Create Entity Consistency

  • Use the exact same name everywhere (not "Datasphere" sometimes, "SAP Datasphere" others)
  • Maintain consistent descriptions across web properties
  • Ensure your About page clearly states what you are in machine-readable ways

3. Build Relationship Signals

  • Get mentioned on authoritative sites (analyst reports, press, partner pages)
  • Create customer evidence with named brands
  • Participate in industry content that defines category relationships

The PMM Imperative

For product marketers, this shift has concrete implications:

  • Messaging must be quotable: Write statements that work as standalone excerpts
  • Positioning must be explicit: Don't assume AI will infer your differentiation
  • Evidence must be specific: Named customers, real numbers, verifiable claims
  • Category must be claimed: State what you are, not just what you do

The PMMs who master this transition will build brands that dominate the new discovery landscape. Those who don't will watch their visibility erode as traditional search gives way to AI-first research.
